title: CV
text:
Dr Rowan Green
I am an evolutionary biologist interested the role of mutation rates and biases in pathogen evolution. I approach these questions with experimental, bioinformatic and quantitative tools. I am committed to collaboration and mentoring with extensive experience managing Bsc & Msc project students. 


Professional experience
May 2026 - Present Killam & BRC Postdoctoral Fellow, UBC, Canada - Studying the nature and evolution of mutational hotspots for the ‘viral cheat’ phenotype in influenza
May 2025 - May 2026 Postdoctoral Fellow, UBC, Canada – Leeks lab – Characterisation of viral diversity in human samples of H3N2 & H1N1 influenza in relation to clinical outcomes
Jan 2025 to March 2025 Postdoctoral Research Associate, The University of Manchester, UK - Krašovec lab - Development of population sequencing based methods for the rapid estimation of microbial mutation rates  
Oct 2022 to Dec 2024 Graduate teaching assistant, The University of Manchester, UK, (Part time) – Workshop facilitation and grading for MSc & BSc modules ‘Reproducible Data Science’, ‘Statistics and Experimental Design’ and ‘Research Skills in Genetics’
April 2021 to Jan 2024 Tutor, The Brilliant Club charity, UK – Independent delivery of university style group tutorials to students aged 12-13 from backgrounds underrepresented in higher education
Jan 2022 to April 2022 Professional Intern, Animal & Plant Health Agency, UK - FAO AMR Reference Centre – Improvement and application of methods for quantifying multi-drug resistance plasmid conjugation rates in agricultural and environmental samples
Sept 2019 to Aug 2020 Program Manager, KEEN Oxford charity, UK – Management of events and volunteers. Creating inclusive social, sporting and artistic communities with people with additional needs


Education
Sept 2020 - Dec 2025 PhD in Ecology & Evolution, University of Manchester, UK - Knight lab - How ecological interactions shape mutation rates to antimicrobial resistance - Awarded 26th Feb 2025– Nominated for Postgraduate Researcher of the Year and Best Outstanding Research Output 
Oct 2016 - June 2019 BA Biological Sciences, First Class, University of Oxford, UK 
Specialist modules: ‘Social Evolution’, ‘Genome Evolution’, ‘Ecology & Evolution’, ‘Tropical Forest Ecology’, ‘Communication, Culture and Collective Behaviour’ & ‘Species Conservation’


External Presentations
Oral presentations: The Social Lives of Viruses, Canada, 2026 (Best Talk Prize); Northern Bioinformatics Users’ Group + Yorkshire Universities Evolution Group, UK 2025 (Best Talk Prize); Population Genetics Group, UK 2022, 2023, 2025; Evolution Joint Congress, Canada 2024; Microbial Ecology & Evolution Hubs, Global with UK hub 2024; Microbiology Society meeting on Understanding & Predicting Microbial Evolutionary Dynamics, UK 2023; SMBE meeting on Prokaryote Genome Evolution, UK 2022
Poster presentations: Influenza Update Meeting, UK, 2025; Microbiology Society meeting on Understanding & Predicting Microbial Evolutionary Dynamics, UK 2025; Society of Molecular Biology & Evolution (SMBE), Mexico 2024; European Society of Evolutionary Biology (ESEB), Czechia 2022


Supervising and mentoring
Since 2021 I have mentored 19 undergraduate honours project and Masters’ thesis students in the UK and Canada. I have supported project conceptualisation, experimental design, data acquisition, statistical analyses and project write up. I have coauthored publications with 7 of these students and have publications in prep with a further 5.


Service

Social events coordinator for ‘Microbial Evolution Research at Manchester’ (MERMan) group 2022-2024. 
Leadership team member R users at the University of Manchester (RUM) group 2023-2025. https://rumgroup.github.io/allaboutrum/
Peer-reviewer for Evolution Letters, PLOS Biology & Microbiology 



Funding

Killam Postdoc Fellowship, Evolution of Mutation Hotspots in Influenza, University of British Columbia, 05/2026 - 05/2028, $120k CAD
BRC Biodiversity Postdoc Fellowship, Evolution of Mutation Hotspots in Influenza, University of British Columbia, 05/2026 - 05/2028, $34k + 7k CAD
BBSRC DTP PhD studentship, ‘How ecological interactions shape mutation rates to antimicrobial resistance’, The University of Manchester, Dr Chris Knight, 09/2020 to 12/2024, £100k (£20k research funds + ~£18k annual stipend)

title: Rowan Green
text:
Hi, I’m Rowan and I study the causes and consequences of mutations in microbes. Some mutations are more likely than others (mutational bias) and I’m interested in how these biases can drive evolution and how they themselves evolve. I’m currently a Killam & BRC postdoctoral fellow at the University of British Columbia where I am primarily working with Asher Leeks on various bioinformatics projects related to the evolution of ‘Viral Cheats’. This largely involves accessing public datasets of viral deep sequencing and using them to reconstruct within host viral populations, my current model systems are human and avian influenza. Prior to this bioinformatics postdoc I have been really lucky to dabble in a wide variety of systems and approaches with my PhD mainly consisting of wet lab microbiology and mathematical modelling, a research assistantship focussed on ecosystem surveying in reforested areas and an honours project surveying pollinators of non-native plants. I am passionate about prioritising reproducible science, mentoring and outreach in my scientific practice.

title: Publications
text:
Full list on google scholar


Green R, Richards H, Ozbilek D, Tyrrell F, Barton V, Zhang Z, Lovell SC, Gifford DR, Lagator M, McBain AJ, Krašovec R, Knight CG. Antimutator and mutational spectrum effects can combine to reduce evolutionary potential in Escherichia coli ΔnudJ. Molecular Biology and Evolution. 2025
This work shows that a single gene knockout can suppress spontaneous resistance evolution, not only through minimising resistance mutations, but also by specifically limiting access to the fittest mutations. Existing efforts to produce antievolution drugs, antibiotic adjuvants reducing bacterial mutation rates, focus on the reduction of mutation rates. This study provides evidence that by introducing mutational biases towards low fitness resistance mutations these drugs could be made far more effective. This study opens the door to the design of NudJ enzyme inhibitors as novel antievolution compounds. I led this collaborative project between 6 research groups, collected the majority of experimental data, mentored 4 junior students to contribute experimental data, carried out all analyses and drafted all manuscript versions. Associated data and code: https://osf.io/mu2ek/
Green R, Bawn M, Angus-Whiteoak A, Jago M, Whelan FJ, Lagator M, Hall N, Knight CG, Krašovec R. Identifying rare spontaneous mutations through wildtype E. coli population sequencing. bioRxiv. 2025 
This work demonstrates the use of deep, population sequencing as an alternative method for microbial mutation rate estimation. This approach overcomes multiple drawbacks of existing methods for mutation rate estimation by combining the rapid, liquid-based features of fluctuation assays with the genome-wide nature of mutation accumulation assays. I led this cross-institution collaboration during a 3-month postdoc with Rok Krašovec, conducting all simulations, bioinformatic analyses, manuscript drafting and organising regular meetings between all authors. Associated data and code: https://osf.io/gztjk/



Green R, Wang H, Botchey C, Zhang SN, Wadsworth C, Tyrrell F, Letton J, McBain AJ, Paszek P, Krašovec R, Knight CG. Collective peroxide detoxification determines microbial mutation rate plasticity in E. coli. Plos Biology. 2024
This study demonstrates the mechanism responsible for the inverse relationship between mutation rates and population density in observed in many microbial species. Using dynamical computational modelling and in culture mutation rate estimation, I show that the negative relationship between mutation rate and population density arises from the collective ability of microbial populations to control concentrations of hydrogen peroxide. Together, these model-guided experiments provide a mechanistic explanation for density associated mutation rate plasticity, applicable across all domains of life, and frame mutation rate as a dynamic trait shaped by microbial community composition. I carried out all mathematical modelling, collected the majority of experimental data, mentored 5 junior students to contribute experimental data, carried out all analyses and drafted all manuscript versions. Associated code and data at the publisher’s website



Jago MJ, Green R, Czernuszka MR, Denisov S, Krašovec R, Knight CG, Lagator M. Extended sequence context shapes mutational bias in Escherichia coli. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. 2026 Jun 9;123(23):e2601345123.
Warner E, Lewis OT, Brown N, Green R, McDonnell A, Gilbert D, Hector A. Does restoring native forest restore ecosystem functioning? Evidence from a large‐scale reforestation project in the Scottish Highlands. Restoration Ecology. 2022 Mar;30(3):e13530.
Warner E, Hector A, Brown N, Green R, Savory A, Gilbert D, McDonnell A, Lewis OT. The response of plants, carabid beetles and birds to 30 years of native reforestation in the Scottish Highlands. Journal of Applied Ecology. 2021 Oct;58(10):2185-94.
I have also been acknowledged on multiple publications for advice with conceptualisation and data analysis including Jago et al, Nat Comms, 2025; Ozbilek et al, MBE, 2025 and Fry et al, Plant Soil, 2025
